over everything on and around the aircraft. Atria staff handle the client; the operator's crew handle the aircraft and the lift.
Loading starts only after the pilot confirms the engine is off and the propeller has stopped.

text.bold: Approved in advance, or it doesn't fly.

paragraph.text: Oxygen, batteries and medical devices need written operator approval.

text.bold: Clients never fly seated in their wheelchair.

paragraph.text: A. Before booking (at least 7 days ahead where possible)

The RN assesses the client and obtains written medical clearance from the client's physician or NP. Flag heart or lung disease, recent surgery, recent stroke or heart attack, anemia, and any air in body spaces (e.g. recent pneumothorax or eye surgery).

The PC-12 is pressurized, but cabin altitude at cruise can be several thousand feet (up to about 10,000 ft at maximum cruise altitude). Ask the physician whether the client needs oxygen in flight, and ask the operator about flying lower if needed.

the client's mobility (wheelchair, walker, transfer method), weight, and height; the weight and dimensions of the wheelchair, walker, and all equipment; medical devices on board; and the number of Atria staff travelling.

Get the operator's written approval in advance for oxygen cylinders, portable oxygen concentrators, power-wheelchair or scooter batteries (especially lithium), and spare batteries. Do not bring any of these unapproved.

Confirm with the operator which device is used: the model, its safe working load, who is trained to operate it, and whether loading is through the forward airstair door or the rear cargo door. Confirm the client's combined weight (with chair, if lifted in it) is within the safe working load.
Confirm ground transport that takes the client's wheelchair, accessible FBO (terminal), accessible washroom at both FBOs, and level ground for the lift.
Confirm whether the aircraft has a usable toilet. Plan toileting before departure and continence products for the flight.
Passports, customs requirements, and medication documents (SOP 52). Atria nurses may only practise nursing where they are registered.
B. Day of travel: before boarding
Arrive at the FBO early so the client is not rushed. Toilet the client before boarding.
Give the pilot a brief: the client's mobility, how they transfer, any medical risks, and where the medication bag is.
Ask the pilot for the safety briefing for the client and Atria staff, including exits, seat belts, and oxygen masks if fitted. Ask how the client would be evacuated in an emergency.

text.bold: Never approach the aircraft until the pilot confirms the engine is shut down and the propeller has stopped.

paragraph.text: Keep clear of the propeller at all times.
Check the ground: no ice, standing water, fuel, or slope at the lift position. Postpone loading in high wind, lightning, or freezing rain.
C. Loading with the lifting device
Only staff trained on that specific lift take part. The lift operator is in charge of the lift; one Atria staff member is in charge of the client.
Inspect the lift before use: platform and guard rails, safety belt, controls, emergency lowering, battery or hydraulics. If anything is faulty, do not use it.
Position the client on the platform facing the direction set by the operator; apply wheelchair brakes; fasten the lift's safety belt or restraint; raise the platform's roll-off barriers.
For a walker user: the client is seated in a wheelchair or boarding chair for the lift. Clients never stand on the lift. The walker travels as baggage.
One staff member stays beside the client and talks them through every movement. Raise slowly; stop if the client is distressed or anything shifts.

At the door, transfer the client to the aircraft seat closest to the door using the method in their care plan and a slide board or transfer belt as needed. Do not exceed manual lifting limits (SOP 32). The cabin height is limited; staff bend at the hips and knees, not the back.
Seat the client in an aircraft seat with the seat belt fastened.

text.bold: Clients do not fly seated in their own wheelchair.

paragraph.text: Fold and secure the wheelchair and walker as the crew directs; nothing loose in the cabin. Remove and keep cushions and loose parts in the cabin with the client.
D. In flight
Keep the client's medication bag, continence supplies, water, and a copy of their care plan within reach in the cabin.
Watch for: shortness of breath, chest pain, new confusion, pale or blue lips, ear pain, nausea, or anxiety. Use a pulse oximeter if the RN has ordered it.
Give oxygen only as prescribed and approved by the operator.
Encourage fluids and ankle and calf exercises to lower clot risk; keep the client warm.
Stay seated with belts fastened when the pilot directs. Tell the pilot immediately about any medical change; the pilot decides on diversion.
E. Unloading and arrival
Wait for the pilot to confirm the engine is shut down and the propeller has stopped.
Reverse the loading steps: wheelchair checked and set up at the door, transfer, secure on the lift, lower slowly.
Check the client for pressure areas, swelling, and how they are feeling before ground transport.

Insurance, accessibility, equipment and medication rules take weeks to sort out.
Atria nurses may only practise nursing where they are registered.

text.bold: Staff are working, not on holiday.

paragraph.text: Rest periods and hours are agreed in writing.
A. Planning (start at least 6 weeks before departure)
The RN assesses whether the trip is safe and what care is needed, and gets written medical clearance from the client's physician or NP for air travel or long trips.
The RN writes a trip-specific care plan: daily care schedule, transfers, medications, risks, emergency plan, and how Atria supports staff remotely.
Decide the number and type of staff needed
for the trip

Atria nurses may only practise nursing where they are registered. Outside Ontario (another province or a US state), check registration rules before travel. If staff are not registered there, they travel in a companion or personal support role only, and the travel care plan says so.

The client buys out-of-province or out-of-country medical insurance that covers pre-existing conditions and medical evacuation; OHIP covers very little outside Canada. Confirm Atria's liability insurance covers staff at the destination.

Confirm accessible accommodation (roll-in shower, bed height, door widths, grab bars), accessible transport at the destination, and rental of equipment there (e.g. hospital bed, commode, lift, oxygen).

Check the destination country's rules for the client's medications; some countries restrict opioids, stimulants, cannabis and sleeping pills. Get a physician's letter listing all medications and diagnoses.

Write down the local emergency number, the nearest hospital with an emergency department, a local pharmacy, the insurer's 24-hour line, the Canadian embassy or consulate (abroad), and Atria's on-call number.
The client or SDM signs the travel care plan and consents to sharing health information with providers at the destination if needed.
B. During the trip
Follow the travel care plan and the client's usual routines as closely as possible.
Check in with the Atria RN or on-call at least daily, and right away for any change in condition, fall, or incident.
Use the same SOPs as at home: falls (SOP 31), transfers (SOP 32), medications (SOP 18 to 20), emergencies (SOP 33).
Adjust for heat, cold, altitude, time zones, and unfamiliar food and water; watch for dehydration, constipation, and confusion.
Check each new room or space for hazards: rugs, bathroom floors, bed height, lighting at night.
Respect boundaries: staff are working, not on holiday. No alcohol on shift; personal time only during scheduled time off.
C. Returning home
The RN checks the client within 48 hours of return.
Reconcile medications, and update the care plan with any changes.
Staff complete documentation and expense reports within 5 business days.
